speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called, I wish to ask the Minister of Finance, in the absence of the Prime Minister, when it is proposed to resume the discussion of the Bill establishing the new province of Alberta ? The Minister of Finance will perhaps remember that my hon. friend the Minister of Justice -who, I regret to learn, has been indisposed for a day or two-made a statement as to what, in his opinion, is the difference between clause 16 as originally inserted in these Autonomy Bills and the amended clause 16, which has not been discussed very much as yet, although it has been before the House for some time. Since the Minister of Justice made that statement-a very carefully considered statement which he read to the House-there has not been any opportunity, so far as I am concerned, to make any observations with regard to it, and if it would be convenient to the government I would like to speak on that question at as early a date as possible. In saying this, of course, I do not desire to put the Minister of Justice to any inconvenience if he is indisposed ; I merely mention it in order that my request ipay be conveyed to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of Justice. I purpose availing myself of this opportunity to bring before the House a matter which is of considerable importance to the province from which I hail. I am quite well aware that in doing so I am trenching upon a policy which has been adopted by this House and by this government of adopting the provincial franchises for the purpose of Dominion elections, and I fancy that so far as that principle applies to the provinces in general it is a good policy. But if I cannot show by the statements which I propose to submit to the House that it is right and incumbent upon the government to adopt a different policy in reference to the province with which I am to deal, then I shall not say anything more about it. It will be within the recollection of those who are conversant with Manitoba politics that in the province of Manitoba adopted in the year 1902 the then government adopted a policy of personal registration; that is to say that every voter, no matter who he was, no matter how long he had lived in the country, no matter how much property he owned, no matter how well known he was, had to come at a certain time to a certain registration booth to register his vote otherwise he had no vote. At the time of the introduction of that Bill I occupied a seat in the legislature and I was very much opposed to the system of personal registration in that way. 1, do not know that there is .such a system in any other part of the empire. If there is I am not conversant with it. The inconvenience of such a system to the province of Manitoba must be manifest to any one who is at all acquainted with its circumstances. The sparse settlement, the long distances it is necessary to travel, the expense, and the inconvenience of it altogether is very much against the system, and the results have shown that the opposition to the system at the time was well grounded. The importance of this subject will appear when I say to* the House that there is not in existence in Manitoba to-day, in one single

constituency for tlie House of Commons, a legal voters' list. We were asked to accept that law because it was commended to us as a new departure, as putting in the bands of tlie judges of tlie county courts tlie compilation of the lists and taking it away from partisan officials. That was the system which was adopted in 1903 in the compilation of the lists. The judges appointed the places for registration, appointed the courts of revision, appointed the registration clerks and all the details in connection with the compilation of the lists were prepared by the judges of the county courts. That certainly looked like a reasonable recommendation. That was continued for a while and the 1903 elections were held upon lists which were compiled in that way. A number of registration booths werp appointed in each local electoral division, a number of days extending from the beginning of the week until the end of the week were given for the time of registration, and in that way although, it was very inconvenient and very expensive and entailed a great deal of work upon the respective parties still a fair, a reasonably fair list under that system was compiled. Now, Sir, I am one of those who think that the government having decided and the Commons having decided by the law of the land what shall qualify a voter, that the voter ought to have the means of registering his vote with the least possible expense and the least possible inconvenience. I think that is a good principle to lay down. Parliament having settled the franchise, having said what the qualification of a voter shall be, the machinery ought to be provided which will enable that individual to get registration or whatever else may be adopted for the compilation of the list and get his name upon the list with the least possible expense and inconvenience. I said that was the system which was adopted in 1903, and the judges of the county courts of the province established the registration booths, completed the lists and the elections were held upon these lists. Previously our law had been that no list would be compiled until prior to an election, so that when a proclamation was issued providing for the compilation of a list it was notice to the public that an election was about to be held and that some time within three months the list would be completed and the election held upon that list. That was the law under the government which I had the honour to lead for a number of years ; that was the law which was introduced by our opponents in 1903 when this system of personal registration was adopted. But Sir, these gentlemen last year, in 1904, conceived the idea that it would be well for them to prepare lists for the purpose of the Dominion election. And they amended the law to provide that the compilation of the lists should take place each vear during the month of May.

They did not make any
provision for striking red lines through it.

I will tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Staples) something about the red lines before I am done. And that reminds me that 1 have to deal with the hon. gentleman before I conclude the remarks I am about to make. If, after I am done, the hon. gentleman will stand up in this House and undertake to defend this iniquitous system, then 1 shall lose what little confidence I have in the hon. gentleman from Macdonald (Mr. Staples).
I can do that with a clearer conscience than that with which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Greenway) can defend his voters' list when he had the compiling of it.

I am dealing with the preparation of the lists under the system established in Manitoba to-day, and I propose to deal with it notwithstanding the interruptions of my hon. friend from Macdonald. Now what did these gentlemen do? The compilation of the list whicfh had been recommended by us because of all the details being worked out by the judges, was at once changed. Instead of leaving it to the judges, an Order in Council was passed, an Order in Council appointing the registration booths, fixing the time when these should be kept open, appointing the courts of revision and settling all tlie details. That was the system adopted by these gentlemen in 1904 for the purpose of preparing the lists to elect such gentlemen as the hon. gentleman for Macdonald. I shall give all the details in order to acquaint the House with the nature of this outrage- there is no other name for it-which is being perpetrated upon the people of Manitoba to-day. Why, Sir, in 1903, under the judges system, when the work was done by these gentlemen who knew the country and knew the circumstances, we had six days of ten hours each for registration. But under this precious system which I am going to discuss in a few minutes, we have one day. Tlie Order in Council which- was passed last month provided that there should be 74 hours of registration. In 1903, when the lists were prepared by the judges, we had 4S0 registration booths in the province of Manitoba-I want my hon. friend (Mr. Staples) to make a note of that-we had 4S0 registration booths open for six days. In 1905, commencing the day after to-morrow, we are to have one day for each electoral district in the province of Manitoba- one day. It was provided by that Order in Council that that one day should be of 7i hours ; but, on account of the public feeling which was aroused in Manitoba, they have now increased it to 13 hours. This, is not, as I will show you later on, a question of time but a question of convenience. Under this new system, we are to have 40 registration booths for the province of Manitoba, instead of 480, and we are to have one day instead of G days. Or reducing it to hours, we had 20,790 hours for registration in

11)03, and in this year of Our Lord, even by the increased time which they have given -they sent out an advertisement after the Order in Council had been passed-they have given just 520 hours. And, in an effort to make it appear that they are doing in favour of the voter they ask them to start at seven o'clock in the morning. Now, that may impress some as being a little unfair, it may occur to some lion, gentlemen who possess a love of fair-play that it is not the thing to do. All I am asking for is fair-play ; all 1 want is that we shall have the means of preparing a complete list of the voters of the province.
Let me give some figures to show how this will work out. I take only a few constituencies, because I do not desire to weary the House. I take ten constituencies out of the total of forty, and give the extreme distances voters will have to travel in order to register their names : Avondale, 40 miles ; Carillon, 78 miles ; Dauplnn, 70 miles. Then I come to the case of Emerson, which is somewhat peculiar. Emerson lies along the boundary, and there is a muskeg or morass in the centre, so that you cannot travel directly from one side of it to the other. People living in some ot the townships of Emerson, in order to register their names, will be obliged to travel by railway to Winnipeg and thence by iaii-way to Emerson a total of 104 miles. In Gimli, a constituency lying to the north, to reach the registration point some of the people will have to travel 21.0 miles , Gladstone, in a somewhat more populous constituency, 110 miles. In Kiklonan and ^t. Andrew's, the home of the old natives of Manitoba, along the Bed river, they have to travel from the extreme points, 260 miles to reach the place where they must register their names; Springfield in the constituency of my hon. friend from Selkiik (Mi. Jackson), 105 miles, Swan River, a Northwestern constituency, 145 miles. Now, Sir, that does not suit even some of the friends of the provincial government of Manitoba, and I do not think it would suit my hon. friend (Mr. Staples) if he had to travel any such distance as I have been speaking of to register his name as a voter. In the other constituencies, the distance varies from to miles to 75 miles. 1 have here a quotation from a Conservative country paper m the constituency of my bon. friend who was interrupting me. Perhaps he knows the paper ; it is the Miami ' Herald published m a nice little town in the constituency of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Staples).
That is the town in which thirteen were disfranchised by the red line.

There are some things that the hon. gentleman talks about concerning which he knows very little. Perhaps he had better send and get a copy of the Miami ' Herald ' if he has not one already. This is what it says :
The new provincial voters' lists are to be made up in June. Carman is the only place for registration in Dufferin. The editor happens to be one of those compelled to drive twenty-one miles and return.
He should not have grumbled, it is a mistake for a gentleman to grumble who has only to go twenty-one miles. That is far below the average, I think he is down at the minimum point.
The editor happens to be one of those compelled to drive twenty-one miles and return or lose his franchise, and we much prefer the latter. We have always been Tory heretofore, but if registered now-well we would feel like putting a government in power that would do the square thing with the registration booth. The prospects are that the Miami boys will stay at home.
Now, Mr. Speaker, why is it that these gentlemen don't want to do the square thing? Simply because of an advantage, which I shall point out directly, that they gain by the compilation of the list of 1904, and they are determined that that list shall remain until they have another provincial general election upon it; they are determined, because the number of unregistered Liberals far exceeds the number of unregistered Conservatives. That is the reason, and I will undertake to prove that to you by some evidence wbicb I have in my possession, giving a comparison between the system adopted by the judges and the system which now prevails. Let me give a few instances with regard to some other constituencies. The first constituency I have upon my memorandum is the constituency in which my hon. friend from Portage (Mr. Crawford) resides, Beautiful Plains. Under the judges system of registration they had 16 places of registration and 90 days for registration, six days for each place; under this government, in 1904, when they were compiling a list for the purpose of electing members of the House of Commons, they gave us 10 places and 10 days. Now, Sir, I want to say here that that was a studied thing, that was the entering wedge that they proposed to drive home upon this last occasion to prevent the peo-

pie from being registered. In the polling subdivision where I happen to reside there was a very large area, 108 square miles, with 320 odd voters in it. It had given the largest Liberal majority that was given in the previous local election, by any single polling division and therefore it must be punished, and they got two hours to do their resignation, from 11 o'clock until 1 o'clock, and one was the dinner hour. That is what they did right at my own home. I went to the gentleman who was registration clerk and asked him who was responsible for this iniquity. He said, not me. I said, I did not think it was. Now, Sir, let me come to the present system of registration and say a word or two about that. I have given you the distances that people have to travel, and I want to show you why it is that these gentlemen have adopted this course ; it is because of the incomplete list, and because they are determined that the Liberals of Manitoba shall not register. In the constituency of my hon. friend from Provencher (Mr. Cyr), and in the local constituency of Emerson, where.I pointed out that it was most inconvenient for electors to register, there are at least 500 available voters for registration, and there will not be 100 of them who will register, there cannot be, there is no provision for it. Let me just remind the House that under the system which we have there is a long list of interrogatories that have to be answered by each person applying to be registered. It does not make any difference who he is, what he is, or how well known he is, he has to answer these interrogatories. It takes quite a time in case there is no dispute over the qualification of the voter, and in case there is a dispute it takes longer. You could not by any possible means register within the thirteen hours that is given by the government, and in a place where there are more than 150 voters it w'ould be impossible for them to register. In the city of Winnipeg, if my hon. friend who represents Winnipeg (Mr. Bole) were here he could tell you that there are available to-day for registration at least from 4,000 to 5,000 voters. Under this precious system it is possible perhaps to register 300 of them, and the remaining thousands have to go unregistered-purposely, systematically it is provided that they shall not register. Why, Sir, I have been surprised when I have been thinking of the manner in which our governments are run, and when I find an old colleague of mine occupying the position of Lieutenant Governor of the province of Manitoba, becoming a party to such an outrage as this,
I cannot find language which I would be permitted to use here, Mr. Speaker, to characterize a thing of that kind. I am free to admit that there is a general idea that a constitutional governor is supposed to do what he is advised to do, but surely there is a limit to that. Fancy a gentleman Mr. GREENWAY.
thirty-five years a resident of Manitoba, who knows all the circumstances, who knows the conditions of the country, putting his signature to a document of that kind, by which at least ten per cent of the electorate of the province of Manitoba are to be disfranchised. I am within the mark when I make that statement. Now, Sir, I want to be perfectly candid with the House, I want to tell the House exactly how things stand. I have the voters' list here which professes to be the voters' list of the constituency of Lisgar. I will say something about that a little later on. We have heard a great deal as to the list and the disadvantage we were placed in by the compilation of it last year when we took no interest in it. I will explain that a little later on. If we were allowed to compile a fair list in Lisgar and if we had a fair list in Lisgar I am here to say in this House that the Liberals would gain at least 300 voters, and shall the doctrine he pronounced in this House or any other House that because they are Liberals they should be disfranchised? Is that a good doctrine to preach? I do not think it is.

I said that as a rule I thought the policy of using the provincial franchise was a good one, but I proposed to show before I sat down that in this case it was not a good one and there ought to be an exception. I said a little while ago that we had not in the province of Manitoba a proper, legal list for any single constituency for the House of Commons. I was quite well aware of it before I came here, but to verify that belief and that opinion I sent a note, after 1 came down here, to the King's Printer and asked him if he would be good enough to supply me with the voters' lists of my own constituency, the constituency of Lisgar. I have in my hand what I received from him and I merely quote this to show the utter impossibility, even if the list were honestly prepared, of using the list which is prepared by the local government for the purposes of the House of Commons. 1 sent over to the King's Printer and he sent me this. You will remember that my constituency comprises two entire local'divisions and parts of three others. I asked the voters' list for my constituency of Lisgar and I received this list. I went over the list which was quite-a little chore and some people of the province of Manitoba got into trouble for doing what I did in reference
MAy 30, 1905
to this about which I will have something to say a little later on. The list 1 received contained 7,344 names. There are 4,237 that belong to me and there are 3,097 that belong to somebody else. How is that ? Take the constituency of Emerson. There is one township in the constituency of Emerson brought into Lisgar and because that one township was brought into Lisgar this gentleman sends me the whole electoral list of Emerson. That applies to Mountain, and to Manitou, two other constituencies portions of which are in Lisgar. If we undertook to hold an election in Manitoba to-day we would not have a list upon which to hold it, and if anybody should undertake to prepare it, because there is no provision under the law by which these lists shall be made, the Attorney General would have him arrested and prosecuted for so doing. I want to say right here that if an election were to take place in any constituency in Manitoba, so long as we have the present Attorney General at the head of affairs, and I were asked to nominate a returning officer for the constituency in which the "election was to be held I would not do so. I would not put my friend in the position of being persecuted as others have been.
Mr. SC I IA IT' X E I t. Ho I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. Greenway) to say that one division of Emerson is brought into Lisgar ?
I did not catch what the hon. gentleman said.
I understand the hon. member for Lisgar to be finding fault because one portion of the local constituency of Emerson was brought into the Dominion constituency of Lisgar.

I did not find fault with it at all. I was finding fault with the list. The hon. gentleman does not understand me. I was finding fault because the list was not right, and I was finding fault because the hon. gentleman's friends persecute people who undertake to put the list right.
I would ask the hon. gentleman to state again what he said about part of Emerson being brought into the constituency of Lisgar.
I said that because one township of Emerson was in the con-constituency of Lisgar, the King's Printer sent me the whole of the list of Emerson.
Exactly, that is what I understand.
I was not complaining about that. I was not saying anything about what the district should be.
That is exactly what I want to know.

The hon. gentleman will know that another reason for complaint
against the Liberals of Manitoba was that they had changed the polling subdivisions. According to the law of Manitoba it was supposed that the registration district under the law which was carried out by the judges should be the polling division. My hon. friend knows, if he thinks for a moment, that one part of the western end of my constituency and one part of the eastern end of his constituency comprise one polling subdivision and that in this subdivison there are 59 votes in my constituency and 142 votes in the constituency of my hon. friend. What is going to be done ? Who is going to provide the remedy ? Who is going to provide that the 59 votes shall vote in my constituency and the 142 in the constituency of my hon. friend ? Somebody has to do it, somebody has done it, and because somebody has done it he has been persecuted and prosecuted by the local government. There have been a great many things said about this election. I know that the Minister of Public Works of the province of Manitoba, who has been quoted sometimes in this I-Ioilse and who has furnished my hon. friends opposite with a good deal of material, has told his friend-S in the east that they propose to carry every seat in Manitoba. Well, he was not without having some good grounds for his faith because he knew how the lists were prepared and he knew that the Liberals had neglected to take part in the compilation. This statement has been made very clearly and perhaps I might as well say here the reason why the Liberals neglected it. I am speaking for the purpose of being perfectly candid with everybody, and I find fault with my friends of the government who knew the state of affairs in Manitoba that they did not carry out their intention at the last session of parliament and give us the means of having a proper list. It was because of the understanding-I never had any personal understanding, but I know I am speaking by the book- that we are going to have a new list that the Liberals neglected the compilation of the list. It was because of the understanding that the government was going to take this course, that the Liberals, in the compilation of the lists, neglected them altogether, and it is because of the local lists which we had that these gentlemen in Winnipeg wanted to perpetuate those lists and get another advantage from them if they could. You could not have a better illustration of how these men acted than a little extract from a paper published in the town from which my hon. friend from Portage (Mr. Crawford) hails. The revision at the court house that paper says, is a production worthy of its authors. This was the revision of 1904 for the purpose of electing members to the House of Commons. Every canvasser upon the Conservative side in Manitoba was told that that was the list upon which the next Dominion elections were going to be run, and they were very eager to see all their friends

get on. Here is one of the results at the Court of Revision :
As a result of the revision 65 Tories were added and 10S Grits were struck off. No Grits were added nor Tories struck off unless in error.
That is a little bit of evidence of how that list was compiled and because this clipping expresses my sentiments, I may as well give it to the House.
But there are fully a hundred Grits that should go on and a hundred Tories that should come off, but it would have cost the Liberals $500 to get their friends on and their opponents off. Such a law is subversive of the liberties of the people and cannot be too quickly wiped off the statue-book. It is the duty of the House of Commons to pass legislation at the present session for a fair and impartial enrolment of the electors for the federal elections.
My hou. frieud talks about the little red line, I happen to know that after we had got the evidence with reference to these lists, we had had the greatest difficulty in the world to get a candidate on our side. I am not revealing any particular party secret that is of much consequence just now when I say that I do know there are sitting in this House, men who declared they would not run because of the failure of the government to carry out the promise which I fancy was made. They were induced to run on account

air. GREENWAY. They were induced to run, and the result was perhaps different from what they expected. X could confront my hon. friend, who interrupted me, with a good deal of evidence on the subject, because it is important perhaps to show the motive of the crime about to be committed next month. Let me refer him to a little inadvertence of his. During the time of the registration for 1904, he received a letter from his leader in Manitoba, of which he did not take that great care he should, or it would not have got into public print. A copy of it was published in some of the papers in Manitoba, and I merely cite this to show that these gentlemen knew then, as they know now, that we did not take any part in the compilation of the lists. I shall not read all the letter but my hon. friend, if he wants to read it through and refresh his memory, can find it in the reading room.
Read it all ; it is not very long.

No, it is not very long, but I need not read it all, because there is a part of it which is not pertinent to the question w'hich I am discussing. For instance that part which refers to my old time friend Mr. Richardson :
I presume you were busy with registration this week, but so far as I can learn no effort is being made by the Grits anywhere. That means Mr. GREENWAY.
one of two things. Either they are going to change the law or there will he no election this year. *
Is that all ?

No, but that is all of that. Then I have here extracts from the Conservative papers in Winnipeg, both senior and junior, crowing over the Liberals because they had failed to have anything to do with the compilation of the lists and then were laughed at by their friends. The ' Tribune,' which is the junior Conservative paper in Winnipeg, and is perhaps a little more zealous than its old time friend the ' Telegram,' because it is its junior, published a long article headed ' The joke of the hour. And the joke of the hour was that the Liberals did not get upon the lists which were to be used in the Dominion elections. It is no wonder then that my hon. friend was disappointed when he found Manitoba went the way it did. And the hon. the leader of the opposition received messages from the gentleman to whom I refer, assuring him that Manitoba would send a solid contingent in his favour.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What gentleman ?
The Hon. Mr. Rogers.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am not aware of any such messages.
I read the messages in the newspapers hut perhaps they did not reach the hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: 1 did not see them.

My hon. friend has been paying a good deal of attention to Mr. Rogers during the session and perhaps it is well he should not forget him just now. A few days after the election, Mr. Rogers came to Toronto and gave an interview, in which he undertook to account for the defeat of tlie Conservative party in Manitoba, in that interview he said :
Three-fourths of the voters in Manitoba were Conservative.
I suppose be meant three-fourths of those who were on the lists, but to a good many the privilege of voting was denied.
In every polling division in the province from ten to forty voters found, on presenting themselves at the polls, that they were unable to vote. Their names were on the official lists and the red line-
This is the red line about which my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Staples) has been dreaming.
The red line had been run through them and the deputy returning officers refused to give them the ballots.
I characterize that as one of the worst pieces of misrepresentation 1 know of. You have only to think for a moment of this fact-There were 545 polling places opened in Manitoba. If I take my hon. friends lowest

number, ten voters, there were 5,450 votes. If I take the average number at twenty, you have twice that; and I want to say right here that in the changing of the lists, which had to be done by some one, there was not in the whole of Manitoba one hundred errors in making those changes. Of course a red line or a blue line, or some other line had to be used to strike out the votes that I refer to. They did not belong to me in Lisgar but belonged to my hon. friend. When I read that,
1 took the trouble to go carefully over the polling books to And out just what happened in Lisgar, and what was the result ? t found that there had been six Liberals left off the list and that three Conservatives had been misplaced. That was the sum total of the errors in Lisgar. My hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Staples) on one occasion undertook to say that his majority would have been vastly increased had it not been for the red line, but I can tell him that if it had not been for the staffing of the lists and for the preventing of Liberals getting on the lists, the hon. gentleman would have had no majority at all.
Now, Sir, I know of no better illustration of the unfairness of the Conservative papers than their action in connection with this matter. Early in the session we had scare head lines in all the papers, from the Montreal ' Gazette' down to the Toronto ' World':
* Frauds in Manitoba ; startling developments in Manitoba in the preparation of the lists.' In my more than a quarter of a century's experience in Manitoba, I do not remember of there ever having been but one special fraud attempted, and that was by a gentleman who was sent up from the east, and whose name was Freeborn, and who came up for the purpose of teaching our people how they might spoil ballots. But upon this last and worst outrage these papers are absolutely silent. Now, Sir, it is not necessary 'for me to go over the entire list of the evidence I have. I have a number of extracts here from newspapers to show that the Liberals neglected the lists entirely. I can give you another very good proof of the fact that the lists were not complete. For instance, in the local election of 1903 there were polled in the province of Manitoba 54,500 votes ; one constituency, Gimli, which was by acclamation, being estimated. In the election of 1904 for the House of Commons, when, by the steady increase which took place in our voting power in a country which is being largely settled like Manitoba, we should at least have had 3,000 votes more, in this Dominion election there was only polled 53,100 votes. Instead of there being 3,000 votes more than in 1903, which would have been the regular increase, there were 1,400 less votes, showing that the lists were not complete, and further giving evidence of the fact that the contention of the premier, when he wrote my hon. friend, was quite correct,
and that we were paying no attention to the lists. That was the position in which we found ourselves. I said a moment ago that ; bad gone carefully over the parts of the country with which I am acquainted and made a very careful estimate of what is the percentage of that incomplete list, and I say now that upon the 1st day of July, when this list is completed by the present arrangement-it has been decreed by that famous Order in Council that it shall be completed within one month, allowing only one day for court revision by the judges in each constituency, making it impossible for people to be registered-when that is all over, ther? will be fully 10 per cent of the electorate of Manitoba that will be disfranchised. I wonder if my hon. friend from Macdonald will undertake to defend that state of things. I do not believe that in the history of Canada there ever was undertaken to be perpetrated upon the people such a gross outrage as' the one we are discussing just now. I bring this matter before the House to-day for the purpose of pressing upon the government the necessity of providing that a proper list shall be compiled for the province of Manitoba. Surely, in face of the evidence I have presented, there can be no hesitation as to the necessity for it. There is no legal provision for the use of the present lists. We all know, and we have the evidence of our opponents, who say that it is not complete. Is there not a spirit of fair-play enough in my opponents, whom I am addressing, to say that there ought to be a means by which every man who is entitled to vote should be placed upon the list ? Is not that good, sound doctrine ?
I think it is. I do not believe that any party would be guilty of trying to fasten-even if they threaten, as they did last year, to sit here till the snow flies-I do not think any party would be guilty of trying to fasten such an iniquity on the people of Manitoba. In view of the evidence I have given, I hope my friends will see their way clear to remedy this injustice. I want to say to our friends here that if we would take the list as we have it to-day in Manitoba, and if we would go to the courts of revision and that it would be possible or convenient to go to in all the towns in the different constituencies, it would cost the Liberal party of Manitoba SI,000 for each local constituency, or $40,000 in all, to make that list perfect. Ought that work be imposed upon any party ? Is it a good, sound principle to force any party to do work of that kind in order to get voters upon the lists ? The system which we have in force now is equal to running two elections instead of one. We have to go to an elector and say : We want you to go to such a place and register your vote ; and he may reply : I will not go. Then you have to persuade him, you have to take him there and see that he is registered, and possibly take him back again ; and then when lie comes to vote you have to repeat the whole

tiling all over. My hon. friends who have teen running elections as long as I have well know something about that. Now, Sir, I do not think that is a fair policy to adopt. X do not think it is fair to our friends in Manitoba. I have spoken longer than I intended and longer than I would have spoken had not my hon. friends opposite interrupted me, but X think I have omitted nothing that is essential to show that the lists are incomplete and that my contention is sound, that they must remain incomplete, because there is no possible way under the system which has been adopted in the province of getting the names on the voters' lists.

1 :fm sorry I had not the pleasure of hearing the whole of the speech of my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Greenway), as I was in .attendance at a committee of the House when I heard that the hon. gentleman was appealing to the jury of parliament in order to get what he calls fair-play, but not what I believe he considered to be the kind of fair-play that he dealt out to his opponents when he was premier of Manitoba. There may be a difference of opinion as to what fair-play is. It is well to remember, however, that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Greenway) has failed to appeal successfully to his own jury in the province of Manitoba ; he was turned down toy the people of his province for all time to come, and now he appears as a private member of the House of Commons and endeavours to enlist the sympathies of the members of this House against what he is pleased to term an iniquitous electoral list. Our friends on the opposite side of the House were not satisfied with \the old Dominion Franchise Act. They said it was too cumbersome and too expensive, and that it put the people to a very great deal of expense and inconvenience, but if we are going to change the present system of preparing the voters' lists, and if we are going to have an inexpensive system, as the hon. member for Lisgar says he desires, then that system should apply to all the other provinces of the Dominion, and should not be specially applied to any one particular province.
Now, however, things have changed; there has been a revolution of feeling, in the more intelligent parts of Canada at any rate, and Manitoba sent the ball rolling in the right direction. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Greenway) would never have held the reins of government so long ias he did in Manitoba on broad questions of public policy. He secured his support at least on two successive elections, by appeals to prejudice and passions of the people toy means of the school question. This is what retained the hon. gentleman in power so very long and not the fact of his general policy being suitable to the people of the province. Now, because they have met with, defeat on a couple of occasions in Manitoba the hon. gentleman desires that an exception should be made in the prov-

ince in connection with the Dominion Franchise Act, and that you should take the provincial lists wherever there is a Liberal government in power and that you should have a new list prepared by the Dominion officials where there is a Conservative government in power. He has in mind no doubt the list that was prepared for the constituency of Lisgar two or three years ago at the time a by-election was held there. The Dominion Act calls for new lists to be prepared by the Dominion officials in the event of the .provincial lists being more than 12 months old. At the time of the by-election Mr. Richardson was seeking the franchise of the electors, and by the way my hon friend referred rather skeptically to his old time friend Mr. ltichardson. Time was when they used to hunt in couples ; time was when Mr. Richardson and the right hon. gentleman himself used to go from hustings to hustings and he appreciated the support that lie received from Mr. Richardson at that time. They are not standing on the same platform to-day.
He has gone Tory.

The fact is that the hon. gentleman and his friends have changed their principles and Mr. Richardson is still standing exactly for the principles that he advocated when he was a candidate for the hon. gentleman and his party. It is the party which has strayed away from their moorings aiid they should not be so very unkind to air. Richardson because he chose to turn his guns on the hon. gentleman now and because standing to his principles, Mr. Richardson in discharging his duties as a public citizen endeavours to lead the hon. gentleman back to his first starting place. There was a by-election in that constituency a few years ago. The provincial lists were more tnan 12 months old and a new list had to be prepared. The Dominion Act states that in the compilation of these lists the provincial law should be followed in so far as it possiblv can be followed. What was the Manitoba Act ? That the judges should prepare the list, should appoint the officials, should have the courts of revision. Was that Act followed out ? Not at all. Mr. Sifton, the Minister of the Interior of that day, ignored the provincial Act in making a new list for Lisgar. This was -one of the cases where that gentleman was superior to the law of the country or thought he was superior, and he therefore appointed not the judges of the province, but one of his own political organizers, a henchman, a private citizen who had been one of his own organizers. He constituted him the board instead of the judges of Manitoba. Was that adhering to the law ? What did he do ? Did he do everything in an inexpensive manner, did he do everything to suit the electors' convenience ? Not at all. He placed the registration booths in the most inconvenient places he could for the Con-

servative party and lie adopted the same plan for tlie courts of revision. He made It as inconvenient as possible for the Conservatives to get on the lists or to get out the votes. The hon. gentleman is sighing for a return to this order of things. He gets up in the parliament here and tries to enlist the sympathy of the members with a tear in his voice telling what wonderful consideration he has for the good old days. He wants to go back to the good old days in Lisgar. when Mr. Sifton manufactured the list through a private citizen, ignoring the judges of the land. He is not so anxious to use the provincial lists as when the Liberals were in power. He says : I desire to see a fair list-and you would think he was in earnest when he says that. His recollection must be very short if he cannot remember when he was Prime Minister of the province, when he used to manufacture the lists. And what kind of lists did we have then. Did he have the judges prepare the lists ? Oh, no. He would not trust the judges in the province. Who prepared the list ? Partisan officers appointed by his own government some of whom had to fly the country for the country's good. I do not have to go at all outside my own constituency to find an illustration of the character of the partisan officials that that gentleman appointed. The law stated that they should take the last provincial lists, the last Dominion lists, and the last municipal lists as a basis in making up the new lists, compiling them therefrom and making any additions necessary, but in making the additions when we were supposed to supply affidavits in the absence of the person appealing for registration, I have myself sent in a list of electors accompanied by my affidavit, that they were legitimate electors, qualified to vote. I handed these affidavits in to an officer appointed by the Liberal government of the day and when the lists were printed a number of these names were left off notwithstanding they were accompanied by an affidavit. This is only one illustration of many, and when the revision was being held and the present Judge Richards was the revising officer, I asked the enumerator who prepared the list how it came that these names were left off. I said : Did you not see that this man's name, (taking one instance), was on the provincial, Dominion and municipal lists and that he had been resident of the province for years ? Why did you leave him off ? Yes, he said, but the laws says I am to get any other information possible that is available. I asked him why he had ignored the passing over of this man's name in the previous lists and had taken outside information. X asked his authority and he refused to give it. I pointed to the Liberal candidate who was there at the time and I said: There ts you authority, you took the word of the Liberal candidate for it that this man's name should not be
on the list, and refused my affidavit. Is that partisanship ? And when the judge, then the revising officer, heard it, he immediately put down the name on the list and called down the enumerator for his partisan action. That is only one illustration of the character of those fair lists that prevailed during the regime of the hon. gentleman who is making such a hubbub about the lists in Manitoba. Take again in the city of Winnipeg. The Ogilvie Milling Company had 30 employees in a certain mill there. These men had been on previous lists, but at this particular time it was found that 27 of the names were left off and three were put on. Of course it was only a coincidence that the three who were put on were Liberals and that the 27 who were left off were Conservatives. When the enumerator was asked how it came that these 27 Conservative electors were left off what was his explanation ? Well, he said, I have an old list to go by, and I found that these three names are on the list and I put them in the new list. He was asked what list he had and he actually confessed it was an old scrutineer's book that had been used in the previous election and he put on the three names that had been marked as voting Liberal and left off the 27 although they all worked in the same mill. And this is the fair list the hon. gentleman wants : to go back to the old days when they did not depend on intimidation and bribery alone but disfranchised the electors by leaving them entirely off the lists. The hon. gentleman has stated that a great many electors in Manitoba at the present time have to go 40, 50, or 60 miles or even more in order to reach the registration courts. And he tells us :	When I was in power
they had so many registration districts, they had so many courts of revision ; two years ago when the judges were running affairs, we had half a dozen or a dozen in each constituency, while now there is only one. In this way, the hon. gentleman compared the revision that is to take place this year with the revision that took place two years ago and when he was in power in Manitoba. But, Mr. Speaker, there is no comparison whatever. Why? Because the list of two years ago was a new list entirely on the basis of personal registration. Those who are already on the list do not need to go up and register again. We have a permanent population, you say. in Manitoba. Of course, there are always new people coming in, but those who, in the meantime, have become qualified, have the privilege of coming forward and registering at the registration booth or at the Court of Revision held some time after the registration, while the names already on the list are left on unless the parties have become disqualified in the meantime and application is made to strike them off. So, the hon. gentleman (Mr. COMMONS
Greenway states only a part of the truth. Why should the country be put to the expense of malting up an entire new list? That is where the hou. gentleman missed having a grievance. Had the provincial government provided for as many registration booths as when the list was being prepared, with all the extra officers and general expense, the hon. gentleman would have been the first to quote this as evidence of the extravagance of the provincial administration. But the provincial government know- that this is an off-year, that there will be no provincial election. Nor will there be a Dominion election, unless the hon. gentleman (Mr. Greenway) is unseated for bribery and corruption, or unless the place of his dear old friend, whom he rather reflected upon, the Lieutenant Governor of the province, which place is to become vacant this fall, attracts him,_ in which event we may have a by-election in Lisgar. But why should the provincial government have the same number of registration districts and courts of revision that they had two years ago when a new list had to be prepared? And the hon. gentleman's comparison of the number of miles electors had to go now to register their names with the number they had to travel for the same purpose two years ago is entirely unfair. The hon. gentleman cannot complain of the Mountain election having been won by unfair lists, because that is one of the constituencies in which the friends of hon. gentlemen opposite had actively looked after the lists, one of the Liberai organizers going there and spending most of iris time last year during the revision. They expected two vacancies in that province. The first was Dauphin, where the Conservative member of the provincial legislature was going to be the Conservative candidate for the Dominion. The friends of hon. gentlemen opposite looked well after that list. Then, they knew that the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Greenway) was discredited as provincial leader, his friends wishing to get him out of the way, were going to put him up as a candidate for the Dominion parliament, which would create a vacancy, in the constituency he then represented in the local House, the constituency of Mountain. And so they looked well after that list. But, in spite of their having a list as favourable to themselves as they could make it, the hon. gentleman's old constituency of Mountain, owing to the great upheaval of public opinion there, defeated his candidate, and, for the first time in twenty-five years elected a Conservative. Two years ago, the judges of the province revised the lists and made the nomination of the registration clerks. And, if fault is found it is found with the appointment of registration clerks by the provincial government to-day. I can only say the gov-Mr. W. J. ROCHE
ernment have re-appointed very many of the men who were appointed two years ago. And, when the hon. gentleman (Mr. Greenway) tries to make his explanation of the ' thin red line,' X think he could hardly have satisfied himself, much less the members of this House. He attempted to show that it was because certain polling districts belonged to two ridings, and that it was necessary to have the names appear according to their proper division. I have here a fac simile of the list for division No. 9 of Selkirk

except that there are black lines instead of red-which I show to hon. gentlemen opposite to make them ashamed of the officials their friends appointed. For, this subdivision was entirely within one constituency, we find no fewer than forty-two names struck off. Many of these men were disfranchised and many more would have been disfranchised had not they taken possession of the poll and insisted upon the deputy returning officer accepting their ballots. But, even when he did accept them, he put them in a separate envelope and did not count them in the general vote. So, when the hon. gentleman attempts to account for this disfranchisement of qualified voters by saying that it was necessary in the ease of subdivisions which are in two constituencies, his explanation does not explain. In my own constituency, the returning officer is an honest, straightforward man, a fellow citizen of my own. He is above doing anything of a dishonest character. But he received instructions from some person. The law states that a returning officer shall prepare, or cause to be prepared, a list which he shall supply to the deputy returning officers and which he shall certify as correct. Did the returning officer for the constituency of Marquette do that? No. My agent waited upon him and saw the lists brought into his office and unpacked. He saw the red line scored through the names and asked the returning officer what explanation he could give of it. The returning officer admitted candidly that he did not do it. My agent asked where the lists were prepared in this way, and the returning officer answered that he presumed that, they were erased in Winnipeg. My agent called his attention to eleven names in a certain district where the voters were wrongly described. For instance, a man living in township 15 range 17 was given as township 16 range 17. And, because of that, red lines were scored through the names. Of eleven names thus wrongly described, ten were those of Conservatives, and all had been scored out. One was a Liberal, and there was no red line through that name, although the description was wrong as in the other cases. My agent asked the returning officer :	How can you
certify these lists to be correct as required by law? And the returning officer answered : I will take good care not to do

anything of the kind ; 1 will write ' certified,' not ' certified correct.' And, ii you will look at the Marquette list, which I moved to have laid on the table, you will [DOT] find that that is the way it is certified. It was a quibble, I grant you; but the returning officer would not take the responsibility of certifying the lists to be correct, because he knew that they were not correct. These lists were scored before they came into his possession and scored in the office of the Liberal organizer in Winnipeg. Now, who were some of these officials ? Take one in the constituency of Selkirk. Everybody will admit that the men appointed to act as deputy returning officers and poll clerks should be men who have the confidence of the people of their districts. But in one district they had a man by the name of Duggan. He had been a bartender in the town of Selkirk. In his evidence he stated that he was a clerk in a hotel, and had previously been tending bar in Selkirk. And this was a gentleman who was appointed returning officer in that constituency, as was shown afterwards in the court. There were at poll 9, Beausejour, twenty-three names struck off; at poll 16 there were twenty-two names ; at poll 11, one name; at poll 26, fifteen names; at poll 27, seven names ; at poll 35, six names ; at poll 37, nineteen names. Some of these may have been put on poll 28, for the list for that subdivision was missing. Many of the lists which should have been sent back to the court were found missing from the ballot boxes and have never been found up to the present day. So far as we can learn, every one of these people was struck off and disfranchised, because they were not all allowed to vote at any poll, though they were entitled to do so.
Now it was invariable, so far as we can learn, there may have been a few exceptions by mistake, but the lists without exception were of Conservative electors. It seems to me that the bon. gentleman was rather venturesome to bring a question like this up in the House of Commons, with such a black record for his party. Not being satisfied with' the thin red line in that constituency, they have used it in other constituencies as well. For instance in the constituency of Macdonald it was not known until the morning of the election by the Conservative portion of the community that these lists had been so doctored, and when they found it out they went to the law officer of the Crown, to the Attorney General and some arrests were made on that occasion. Investigations have been held and some of the charges have been thrown out on technicalities, for instance in one case where the charge was that they wei'e erased from the list the word ' wilful ' was left out, and on this the judge threw the case out because he held it was an error or omission. But there were other cases that never came to trial because the grand jury did not allow, as I think they
should have allowed, in my opinion-I am not going to accuse them of being animated by political motives-but at any rate the grand jury did not see lit to allow other cases to come to trial. Nevertheless these gentlemen, through another process of law, are going to be made to face the music, and we will see if they can commit these crimes with impunity. I might read a great deal of evidence distinctly declaring that the witnesses had taken their lists into Mr. Leach. And who is Mr. Leach '! Mr. Leach was the Dominion Liberal organizer for the province of Manitoba. He has since secured his reward by being appointed to a position in the Department of the Interior, the usual refuge for all these gentry who were doing handy work for the Liberal party. Mr. Leach is to-day in the employ of the Dominion government as a reward for his political services. He opened an office in the city of Winnipeg, he had the returning officers send or bring their lists into him, and he even prepared the proclamations. These proclamations were prepared some time prior to the election by means of a personal canvas, and the canvas books were prepared throughout the province by the Liberal organizers long before the elections were held. In my constituency there was a gentleman by the name of McNab who had never been out of the constituency prior to holding the election, for 10 months doing just such work preparatory to scoring off those names. These lists were prepared under the direction and guidance of Mr. Leach. Can any hon. gentleman on the opposite side of the House defend that proceeding ? Who can say that it is right and proper for the Liberal organizer to take this work out of the returning officers hands, the gentleman who is by law appointed to prepare these lists ? They are taken entirely out of his hands by the Liberal organizer, and do you suppose that a gentleman of that kind is likely to do his work in a manner to commend itself to the fairness of both political parties ? Is it surprising that under these circumstances we find the thin red line doing its work very efficiently in many cases ? Let me read the evidence of one Ayotte, a deputy returning officer, when he was being cross-examined. He states that he took his list into the office of Mr. Leach, the Liberal organizer, who furnished him with his proclamation and asked him if he could fix the lists according to the proclamation, and he said he could. He is asked :
Did you leave the lists with him ?-A. Yes, sir.
Shortly afterwards he went back to Mr. Leach and obtained the lists altered in a great measure by having lines struck through names on the lists. He apparently did not take the trouble t^p ascertain whether the alterations made were proper or not, nor did he even examine them for the pur-

6^60
pose of ascertaining what were the nature of the alterations Mr. Leach had made, for he goes on in his evidence to state :
Mr. Knott : Q. You did not know anything about thorn, that is, the lists ?-A. No.
Q. They may have been different lists altogether for all you know ?-A. Yes.
Q. They may have been lists for Macdonald or Winnipeg ?-A. Yes, they may have been.
Q. You took his word (that is Mr. Leach's) that these were the lists you wanted, with the different polling subdivisions, and that satisfied you then ?-A. Yes.
Having received the lists in this altered condition, Ayotte certified to them as being correct, although he admitted he did not know whether they were correct or not. He then went and placed them in their respective ballot boxes, which ballot boxes he had kept in the Liberal candidate's committee rooms in St. Boniface. The Liberal committee rooms in St. Boniface were the headquarters for this gentleman, where he took his lists and left them in their boxes. All the official papers transmitted to him in connection with the election from Provencher were also kept by him in Mr. Cyr's committee room in St. Boniface, but how long they were there the witness could not tell. There was no safe there where they could be locked up, and it is not known bow many people had access to them during the time they were there. He did not know just how long they remained in that committee room. Now this gentleman confesses that he took the lists to the Liberal organizer ; and be took them to be fixed in conformity with the proclamation, and that Mr. Leach had them fixed for him. He went and received the lists, without knowing whether they were the same lists, then he left them open in his box in the Liberal committee room where they remained until the election. Now if that is the kind of fairness the hon. gentleman wishes to re-establish in the province of Manitoba I do not think the people of that province of either political party will agree with him. I do not think it is necessary for me to read all this evidence. Probably some time we will have an occasion to go into this matter more fully. The hon. gentleman from Lisgar (Mr. Greenway) has seen fit to leave the House, therefore I do not think I need trouble you with any further quotations. I desire to say that there is no comparison whatever between the lists as prepared to-day under the Conservative government, in respect to fairness, and the lists that were previously made by the Liberal government. There is no responsible citizen in Manitoba, no matter what his polities, who would desire to go back to the old sy stem, if you read the independent press of that province you will find them stating alniost without exception that although the original lists may have taken a little more trouble to prepare, they were sure to be clean lists, and people could be sure that they did not contain the names of dead men, Mr. W. J. ROCHE.
of men who had been absent for years, as | was the case with the lists prepared by the j agents of the Greenway government. People prefer to vote on clean lists, even though they are a little more expensive on account of various registrations that have to take place. Therefore there is no possible comparison between the present lists and what they were a few years ago. The Greenway law required the lists to be made just prior to a provincial election, once every four years. The present law provides for an annual revision and immediately prior to a general election a more complete revision will take place and the people will have all the registration districts they require. But this year's revision is merely supplementary to the original lists. I think when the speech of the hon. member for Lisgar is published in the province of Manitoba it will not meet with much approbation.

Mr. Speaker, I was rather pleased with the remarks of the hon. member, for Marquette (Mr. Roche) who has just taken his seat because of the fact that what he said went a long way to prove the point which my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Greenway) attempted to make. I noticed that he failed to defend the position that he now occupies in so far as our Franchise Act is concerned and in so far as the conduct of the government of the province of Manitoba is concerned. There is no question but that the condition of affairs as it exists at the present time by reason of the adoption of the provincial lists of the province of Manitoba is far from what it ought to be. The remarks of my bon. friend from Lisgar, I think, in every particular, embodied a true statement of tile facts. I will try simply to enlarge upon the statement lie made. I may just say before proceeding with the few remarks I intend to make that we expect that our friends on this side of the House will seriously study the situation, and that our friends on the other side of the House will do the same. I believe I am not going beyond the true state of things when I [DOT] say that this side of the House is not wholly 'responsible for the condition of things prevailing in Manitoba at the present time. thinks that when the list is over one year -old it will not be a fair list, that there will be men on the list whose names should go off because they had left the country, or men might have come into he country in the interval and would be entitled to vote. So, Mr. Roblin went a step further. On the occasion of making the first list every citizen of Manitoba who wanted to vote at the coming election had to register his name so that you can understand it would take' a considerable time, and 1 want to say, because I went through it and know something about it, that there was ample opportunity afforded. I am not speaking for Winnipeg, but I am speaking for the rest of the country when I say that we could have registered three or four times as many men as we registered during these six days. I want hon. gentlemen to understand that what I have described is the system of registration all along the line. That system was new but I want to say and I say it without fear of contradiction that there was very little complaint about it from Grit or Tory and that they were well satisfied with it. But, it was new and some electors said : I have been in the country a long time and I am not going out to register. So, for that reason, at the first registration, it was not possible to get all the qualified names on the list. So the next year Mr. Roblin said : I will give you one day, but I will give you six places. A gentleman was appointed, he went around to these six places in each small county after due notification had been given to the voters of the district that they could go and register their votes. That does not look very much like an attempt to keep qualified voters off the list, and it is a fact that they could have registered a great many more names. Is it not fair to believe that after the previous registrations which had taken place the registration of last year would not require so much time ? But, nevertheless, hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House complain of how far men had to travel in order to register their names. I think I am correct in saying that they did not have to travel any farther than they had under the Greenway registration because under the Greenway registration there was only one place to register, whereas there are six to-day. There may have been a few exceptions to that, but there were very few. I think any hon. member who followed the argument of my hon. friend from Lisgar will agree with me that it bears out the expression I made use of at the beginning of my address to this House when I said that he was talking against time and trying to defer the consideration of something that is more important than the question which he has brought up. The voters whose names are on
the list absolutely do not have to register. No one has to register if he is already on the list. Only those who have become qualified since the last registration are required to register. I would ask this House to compare these two systems of registration.
I have tried in as few words as possible to put before the House the system of registration prevailing in the province of Manitoba and I am confident that this House will agree that the remarks of the hon. member for Lisgar are very uncalled for.

When you left the chair at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was replying to the attack made by the member for Lisgar (Mr. Greenway) upon the Manitoba voters' lists. I said that I believed this Question was brought before the House this afternoon by gentlemen opposite in order to postpone the discussion on the Autonomy Bill, and in that effort I propose to be generous enough to help them to some little extent. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Greenway) tried to make out that the system of preparing the electoral lists in Manitoba was unfair and unjust, and my remarks were directed to prove that the registration under the Roblin government was far more effective and in every way fairer than the system under the Greenway government. The question is important and at the risk of wearying the House I shall explain the conditions in Manitoba. The topography of that province is different from that of either Quebec, Ontario or the eastern provinces. Beginning at the south eastern end of Manitoba we have ranges running from east to west and townships which are gjx miies square running from north to south. The average local constituency in the thickly settled portions would include about three ranges from east to west making 18 miles, and about 0 townships north and south or 36 miles. To show how fair the Roblin government was and how anxious it was that there should be sufficient time given for registration, the constituencies were laid off, in my part of the country at all events, into what might be called three tiers. There was first the registration clerk for the whole constituency and under him there were officers known as clerks. In the constituency which I have in mind there were three clerks in the north end, three in the centre, and three in the south making 9 clerks to register the names. They worked from iron day morning until Saturday night, their offices being open until 10 o'clock at night in order that working men might register, and I say without fear of contradiction that after the legal hour for closing at night not a single name was put on the lists. There was an absolutely new votei-s' list being prepared, and so we commenced with a clean sheet and every one had to register. I can say that had twice as many voters come forward to register, ample time was given to enable them to do so. Contrast that with the Greenway system under which in the local constituency of Turtle Mountain there was only one man to register, and he was located at Boissevain, to which town every voter had to come to
