We had enumerators who compiled the lists when the late Greenway government was in power. It was the duty of those gentlemen to take the municipal lists as a basis. That is what they did ; and if we had an election law anything like the election law you have in Ontario, I would be perfectly satisfied to accept it. Take any list as a basis. Take the municipal lists. Then let the manhood suffrage voters be put on by the judge at the court of revision. There is great objection to this personal registration. Take old timers who have been on the lists some twenty-five or thirty years, they have to come and register. During this campaign, I met one of the prominent residents of Winnipeg, who is living in the district of Kildona, which is a suburb of Winnipeg, but is in the division of Selkirk. He was a Conservative too. I went in to see if I could get his vote, and he said he would be very happy to vote for me but he had not registered, and that the present Roblin government list was an outrage. That Roblin law compels men who have owned property in the country for years and who have been on the lists some twenty or thirty years to go and register, and hundreds of them said : We are entitled to be on the list, why should we travel ten or twenty miles to register ? We had enumerators in Manitoba who went around and took all the voters they could, and I may tell you what we did in our part of the country. I held a series of meetings, just meetings for the purpose of getting

everybody to attend and register and have his name on the list. I wanted their names put on regardless of politics, but the people have to come and register, and they do not know to-day what the law is and are in doubt whether they will be on the list. The kon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) said that the law is only there for the purpose of adding to the list, but when did they change the law ? As far as I understand the law, it requires personal registration in every case. It is just optional to-day with the registration clerk to put names on the list or leave them off, and the clerk is there for the purpose of registering. I am not aware that the law lias been changed so as to enable those men who are now on the list to stay on.
The law absolutely states that only those who have become qualified since last year, who have become British subjects, or have been in the province long enough to vote, need register this year.
What about the thousands who were qualified before last year and who are not on ?
Is it not their fault if they do not get on ?

No, because they may have to travel fifty, sixty and sometimes 260 miles in the county of Selkirk to register. From Fisher river they have to travel 150 miles, from Black Island, 100 miles, from Bad Throats, 100 miles, from Gimli sixty miles, and that is the only way by which they can be put on the list. They have to travel by team and by water, with no regular boats running. There is one thing which the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) brought up this afternoon and which I do not think he was justified in bringing up. He tried to leave the impression on this House that the returning oflicer for the county of Selkirk during the last election was a bartender. I do not know whether he meant it or not, but he said it. I might just point out that when I was asked to name a returning oflicer, I settled that the proper place from which to select that official was the town of Selkirk because it was in the centre of the county. I was not there at the time myself, but I sent word to the Liberal Association to appoint a returning officer. They appointed a gentleman called Lawrence Duggan. His appointment was perfectly satisfactory to me.
Hear. hear.

Yes, I have known him for some five or six years. He is not bartender ; his half brother Martin O'Donohoe is the local member for the same county and he owned the hotel where this gentleman acted as clerk, and I dare say he may have gone behind the bar and sold a drink although I do not know that I ever bought one
from him. However, he is as respectable a man as any gentleman in this House. I have known him for years, he does not drink himself and he is a good young man. I may also say that he has been out of the business for over two years. At the time of the election he was a clerk in a store in Selkirk, and I defy any gentleman in this House to say that before he was appointed returning officer or since, Mr. Lawrence Duggan was not a man of excellent character. The federal division of Selkirk comprises the whole of four local divisions and the local divisions returned three Conservatives by majorities of over 100 each, while I carried each of these divisions by about 125 majority. The Roblin government wanted to put some courage into their supporters and so they made charges against certain Liberals that these gentlemen were not guilty of. It is needless to say that these indictments were thrown out by the grand jury. They have now instituted proceedings against Mr. Duggan and Mr. Leach but they are not able to prove anything against them, and will not be able to prove anything because I am satisfied that everything is as straight as it possibly could be so far as Mr. Duggan is concerned. The Liberals thought of course that the county of Selkirk was stolen from them, because they had the lists so loaded in their favour that they believed they were certain of carrying the constituency. Bitt, Sir, it was the policy of the Laurier government that was so popular in that country that carried the election, and it secured for me hundreds of Conservative votes, and these Conservatives would vote for me again if there was an election tomorrow. Indeed, if the lists were fair it would not be a majority of 500 that I would have, but a majority of at least double that. I can tell these gentlemen opposite that the policy of the Liberal government is so popular in the west, that if there was an election there now, the Liberals would carry ten seats.
Why did'nt you carry Mountain ?

That is easily explained. I can give you a little information about that if you want to know. The five members of the Roblin cabinet were up there and they had every civil servant working for them, and three or four surveying parties were laying out ditches and offering $1,000 here and $1,000 there if certain districts gave good majorities for the government. In one particular municipality where there is a local option, the people'wanted a license and the friends of the Roblin government told them that if there was a good majority for their candidate they would put them into a new municipality so that they could get a license. I cau tell my hon. friends that the educational clauses of the Autonomy Bill, or the boundary question did not figure in that election.

For the benefit of the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Sehaffner) I wish to read the Manitoba electoral law which says :
21. Lists of electors shall hereafter only be made and revised at such times as is hereinafter provided :
(a)	Provided that a new list shall he made and revised in the case of every general election ;
(b)	Provided also, in this case of a by-election, the list last revised under this or any previous Act may he used if not over one year old. If over one year old, a new list of electors shall be prepared for the electoral division affected.
This law says that a new list shall be made.
What is the date of that statute ?
That has been changed.
There is no amendment to that so far as I am aware, and there is nothing to hinder the Roblin government striking us all off the lists if we do not appear.
The hon. member knows that is not correct.
I do not. I have read the law for you.
That is the law of 1901.

Then point out any changes that have been made. I think the hon. member for Marquette should apologize to Mr. Duggan ; he is not a bartender ; he has had nothing to do with a bar for a year and a half, and he was never in the real sense of the word a bartender at all. I have a number of very warm friends who have been in that business, and 1 dare say hon. gentlemen opposite are in the same position. I think it has been clearly proven that we have an iniquitous election law at present in Manitoba. I want a fair list; I want to see justice done to voters irrespective of politics, and I say that it is the duty of this government to give us a revision of the lists, taking the local lists as a basis and having a revision by impartial judges. I do not want any partisan revising barristers. I want to see the lists prepared by impartial judges. When we have a government such as that now in power in Manitoba who will not give us fair voters' lists, but who have loaded itp the lists in their favour and are trying to keep them in that shape, then it is the duty of this government to remedy that even if we. have to stay here till the" snow flies. It is the duty of this government to see that every voter in the Dominion of Canada who is entitled to vote should be put on the voters' list regardless of politics, and even though we have to stay here till Christmas or January next, justice should be done.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that he wants an exception made of Manitoba in this respect ?

It may he necessary to extend it to the province of Ontario in a short time if the Conservative government there do not render justice. We may not he alone in the time to come, but I do say that in view of the government we have in power in Manitoba to-day, an exception should be made for that province. If the Manitoba government would give us a voters' list similar to that in Ontario I would be satisfied. but if they adopt the partisan system under which they can favour themselves if they have a clerk that is any way crooked, then that should be (prevented. In the town in which I registered I have myself seen dozens of men to whom the oath was never administered and who were put on the lists, while dozens of other men were sworn. As I understand it the law says that a man can not he entered on the lists unless the man who proposes to put him on swears that he was unable to he present or was away from the country or something of that kind, but names were put on the list right along in my town without that precaution having been taken. This shows how loose the system is. It is the duty of this government as soon as possible to introduce an Act making an exception for the province of Manitoba, and giving us what we consider would he a fair list ; let the judges do it.

AT,OR. The hon. gentleman has stated that in some cases people lived so far away that it is impossible for them to register. Is that not as fair for one party as the other ; do not Conservatives live as far away from the polls as Liberals ?

I have always been in favour of making it convenient for the people, whether Conservatives or Liberals and I think we should not compel even Conservatives to come down 260 miles to register their votes.
Do they travel any further under this system than under the other ?
Yes.
Why?

We had an enumerator who went around and put their names on, and there were very few put on at the court of revision. There were lots to strike off, as the hon. member for Souris said this afternoon, but very few to put on, for the list as a basis, there were always men on and there was only the cleaning of the lists to be done.
Why were there so many to strike off ?

With the municipal list as a basis, there were always men on the list who were dead or who had moved away, because they are marked residents

for certain purposes of statute labour. There used to be trouble about that when we took the municipal lists as a basis, and in that way we had to clean up the list.

I am sure anything I may have to say, coming from an ordinary farmer like myself, cannot be so interesting as remarks would be coming from an hon. gentleman like the hon. member for Selkirk. That hon. member went up to Manitoba only a few weeks ago, and by hanging a map on the wall, taking a pointer and making a few scientific flourishes with it, he solved the whole boundary question that has been troubling the people of Manitoba. If he was so effective in solving the boundary question, I think we can afford to have the solution of the Franchise Act of Manitoba put in his hands. His solution would be about as effective as his solution of the boundary question of Manitoba. The hon. gentleman has been finding fault all afternoon with the registration that is taking place in the province of Manitoba, that is the annual registration. If we were under the Franchise Act of the Greenway government we would have no registration at all this year, because it was not annual as at present, and those men who are desirous of getting on the list would not have an opportunity of doing so if we were under the Greenway Act. All they have to do now is to go to the registration booth and, as has been pointed out to-night, it is as fair for one as for another. The hon. gentleman went on to say that if the lists had not been stuffed, instead of there being seven representatives here supporting the government to-day there would be ten. I want to say that if it had not been for the mutilation of the lists for Selkirk, if it had not been for the thin red line and other things of the same nature, he would not be here to-day, and I would say further that if he has a spark of principle, knowing the conditions and the methods which were adopted in order to secure his election, if he is the gentleman I think he should be, he would resign his seat and say : I did not win that election fairly and I wish to contest it over again. Talk about how he got here, about the striking out of names ; there were forty-two Conservative electors struck off at one division, and he took good care that he did not mention that there were a number of polling booths in that constituency where the Conservatives went in numbers asking for ballots and were refused, and were told that there was a red line through their names and they could not vote. The hon. gentleman knows that, and he also knows that in several polling subdivisions where they asked for ballots and could not get them, they became boisterous, forced the doors, demanded a ballot and made the deputy returning officer give them a ballot and take back the ballot. As a matter of fact, what did he do? He would not allow them to deposit the ballots in the 216
ballot box, but he put them hi an envelope, and, if I am rightly informed, they again went into the booth after reconsidering what he had done with the ballots and forced the deputy returning officer to tear the end off the envelope and drop the ballots one by one into the ballot box. You talk about your ballot stuffing, your ballot switching and your bogus ballot boxes, but there is nothing to my mind, or to the mind of any fair elector, equal to the thin red line. A more effective scheme could not be thought of, and this scheme I have mentioned has been utilized, and what does the hon. gentleman ask to-day ? They know they cannot go back and practise the same device, and come here asking this government to pass a special Franchise Act for Manitoba, whereby they would be able to exercise other schemes in order to be elected. It has been explained how our lists are compiled, and I have yet to find a Liberal in Manitoba who will not say that the (present list there is the most fair and just that has ever existed in the province. Ask any Liberal in my own constituency, and he will tell you this. The gentlemen who have spoken this afternoon know full well that	this
subject has been debated on the floors of the local legislature, and the leader of the opposition there has stated that it is a fair compilation of the list, but that it is too expensive ; that is the only fault he has to find with it. The hon. gentlemen say that the red line had to be used. Admitting that the red line had to be used, although I do not think it was necessary to use it, had this government taken hold of these lists at the proper time and compiled them here, then it would not be necessary to use the red line. The red line is all right if it had not been abused, but up go the lists, and'where do those lists go to ? Before going to the deputy returning officers throughout Manitoba, the lists went into the hands of one Mr. Leach, who sat in the Liberal committee room in Winnipeg and drew the red line just where it suited his own will. Where is this gentleman, Mr. Leach, to-day ? He is under the employment of this government, as some one has well said, receiving his reward the same as many others. The hon. gentlemen who have spoken on the other side have evidently been preparing this subject. Each came here with a long brief and a pile of papers.
I had secured and gathered together a number of papers relating to this subject which I have handed over to another hon. member on this side who is unfortunately away from the House this evening, and 1 have not the information and the facts with me that I might have presented to you to-night. I know the subject will come up later on, and then there will be plenty of time for stating facts. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. S. J. Jackson), who was in the constituency of Mountain in the campaign which recently took place has ven-



tured the statement that the school question was not made au issue there. If the hon. gentleman will go through the archives of this country and search the papers printed and speeches made in that constituency, he will find that the school question and the boundary question were the two issues upon which the constituency of Mountain was won by the Liberal Conservative candidate.
I am glad that we have at last heard from the hon. mernDer for Lisgar (Mr. Greenway). He has sat here through this entire session which has lasted almost five months, and not a word have we heard him utter until this afternoon, But I venture to say that when the newspapers appear in Manitoba to-morrow they will contain some expressions of surprise that he has waited all this time to deal with such a question as this after having missed so many opportunities to deal with a question of more importance-though this one is important too. Why have we not heard from the hon. gentleman (Mr. Greenway) on the school question, a question on which he was returned to power time and again and upon which this government rode into office ? The people of Manitoba, I venture to say, would much prefer to hear him talk on that question than on the question which he has made the subject of his first speech in this parliament.
Now, I wish to call attention for a moment to the way that this ' thin red line ' did its work in the constituency of Macdonald. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Greenway) seemed anxious to draw attention to me and spoke of the little town of Miami. I wish to call attention to one incident that occurred there. On the 4th of November last, there were thirteen Conservatives went to the poll there and asked for ballots that they might vote for the Conservative candidate. Did they get them? They were coolly told that there was a red line through their names and that they were disfranchised. The statement has been made that they were probably on the list in some other division. They were not on the list in any other division, and I defy the bon. gentleman to prove to the contrary. But Miami is not the only place in which such things occurred. Take the polling subdivision at Poplar Point, and there the names of fifteen men had the red line drawn through them, men who had lived in that polling subdivision for years. Of these men every one was a Conservative. The same was true at Miami-every one of the eleven who were disfranchised was a Conservative. I have gone to considerable trouble to ascertain how many men were disfranchised In the different polling subdivisions of Macdonald, and I find that close upon 300 Liberal-Conservatives who went to the polls and asked for ballots, found that their names has been erased. I may also cite the case of a Liberal who. just before the election, meeting a Conservative in my town, said : 1 Well we have got Sta-Mr. STAPLES.
pies trimmed.' My friends replied : ' It is not possible. .' But the answer was : 'You will find out that what I say Is right, and when the polls are closed you will see the basis on which I make the assertion.' It was on the ' thin red line ' that this man based his prediction. They went it pretty strong ; they went it to the extent of nearly three hundred ; but they did not go it quite strong enough. Now, just one other point with regard to my own town Tre-herne. This is a matter that came under my own observation. On the day of the election, two electors went to the poll and asked for ballots. They were told that there was a red line through their names. They came to me and asked how it was. I told them that possibly they were outside the limits indicated by the proclamation. I went to the polling booth expecting to find a copy of the proclamation, but there was none though the law requires that one shall be hung in the polling booth. After a little time I succeeded in getting a copy which I took to the deputy returning officer and told him that these men lived within the hounds of the polling subdivision and that he could not legally refuse them a ballot. Though, for a time he refused, I must admit that these were fair men-about the average of Liberals after considerable argument, I succeeded in getting ballots for the voters who had been refused them. And they voted, I suppose that had the case arisen In some other polling subdivision I could not have succeeded for in all these polls I had good scrutineers who asked the officer to allow the electors to use their franchise, but they refused.
Now, I am satisfied that this question will come up later on and I have something to. say about it, for I have plenty of information on the subject. But before I take my seat I wish to call the attention of the House and country to what one Liberal newspaper has said as to the fairness and justice of the method of compiling the voters' list in use in Manitoba. I quote from the ' Eye Witness,' of Birtle, a newspaper which, I understand, is edited by a good Liberal :
The Winnipeg ' Free Press ' is working overtime endeavouring to make a mare's nest of the Manitoba Franchise Act. Had it expended half the energy during the twelve years its friends were in power urging them to give the province something better than the cemetery voters' -lists that were used until Roblin's government enacted the present personal registration Bill which, while not perfect, is without doubt the best franchise law anywhere in Canada, the Liberal piarty would now have something in this line creditable to look back to. The * Free Press' present harping Is so out of place that every Liberal paper in the province, except its couple of echoes, are discreetly silent. A few columns on red line disfranchisement would be more to the point.
I do not think for a moment that, when all the facts are known as to the method of compiling the lists in Manitoba this House will think of enacting a special law

for that province. As this newspaper states, we have the fairest method of compiling these lists used anywhere in Canada. It is a credit to Manitoba to have such a system. At-the same time, I am satisfied, that as time goes on, it will be made even more perfect.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not rise for the purpose of participating in the discussion in regard to what has occurred in the province of Manitoba, for. like many other hon. members of the House, I have no knowledge of the facts except as they have been presented in this discussion. I wish to say that I think the principle upon which the Dominion Franchise Act is framed is one in the interest of public economy and public convenience. The preparation of a second list for Dominion elections throughout the whole Dominion would involve a considerable expense. But that to my mind is not the most serious side of* the question. Everybody who has anything to do with political organization must know that the preparation of an electoral list involves a great deal of labour and time to many of the best citizens of our country, and I count among those all who take an active and intelligent interest in public affairs on either side of politics. The time that is spent and the labour that is involved in getting up electoral lists are therefore considerable, anl I think we could all agree that if we can minimize that labour and sacrifice throughout the Dominion, by having one list instead of two, such a condition is very desirable. Whether we have attained perfection in that respect under our present system, may be a matter of debate. While I would contend that the present system on the whole has a good purpose and works well, if it could be shown that the system is abused in any province, by any government, Liberal or Conservative, and that the intention of this parliament respecting the free exercise of the franchise by every elector of this Dominion Is not being carried out, but that there is a deliberate and systematic abuse of the system with a view of disfranchising any portion of the electors, then I think we would all agree, irrespective of politics, that a remedy should be provided. Whether that condition has been disclosed in the province of Manitoba, I confess I have not sufficient knowledge to express an opinion. I can only say that in view of what has been presented to the House this afternoon, the matter is one of great gravity, and I feel that the principal law officer of the government, the Minister of Justice, should give the matter full consideration, and I have no doubt he will do so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
acknowledged, what some of their friends denied here last session, namely, that it was proposed to pass by the lists so made up, with an appeal to judges, as I understand is the case in Manitoba-to pass by those lists and have other lists made up in that province by partisan officers, in order that a certain advantage might accrue to their political friends. We had the intimation also later on that there were certain members of the cabinet for whom a proposition of that kind was a little too strong. The hon. gentleman for Lisgar and his friends to-day spoke somewhat tearfully and regretfully of the circumstance that their proposal was not adopted by the government. I am glad for the credit of some members of the administration at least, that they found a proposal of that kind a little too strong ; I am glad of it for the sake of public life in Canada, and for the credit of some members of this administration in that regard. Here were lists that could be revised by independent officers, lists as to which there was an appeal to judges in the province of Manitoba. And I may say in passing that we vainly fought in this House for similar appeals in respect to provincial lists in the province of Nova Scotia, and members of the administration -would not permit us to have even that. But here were lists that were revised by independent officers, in respect of which an appeal would lie to the judges ; and the proposal coolly admitted by the gentlemen who have spoken on that side of the House, was that these lists made up by independent men, subject to revision by judges were to be passed over in order that lists might be manufactured by partisan officers. Well, if that is what my hon. friend the Minister of Finance says is under consideration by the government-I do not know whether I am to interpret his remarks in any other way-I venture to say that if he brings down a proposal of that kind, after once having committed himself and his government to the principle of leaving these matters to provincial legislation, any measure of that kind will be before this House of Commons for a very long time before it will pass.
There are many things which the opposition has to concede to the majority in this House. The rights of the minority in this House are not always regarded as absolutely sacred, but when highway robbery of that kind is suggested, because that is what it amounts to, I venture to think that the hon. member of Lisgar will find that they have attempted one of the most stubborn and difficult propositions that they ever endeavoured to put into force, and it is just as well that this should be understood before the government are committed to any proposal of this kind. We took our stand upon the principle which has been advocated by the Conservative party. We made no factious opposition to the proposi-Mr. R. L. BORDEN,
l
tion which was brought in by this administration when they changed the method of making up the lists ; but when it is said that you shall have one principle for making up the lists in a province which happens to have a Liberal administration and another principle for a province which happens to have a Conservative administration and that there shall be one principle applied to provinces like Manitoba and Ontario in respect, and an altogether different principle to Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and other provinces where there is a Liberal administration-to say that we are to have anything like that in this country is going a little bit too far, and I venture to think that the administration upon reflection will think twice before they accede to the proposition which has been coolly and unblushingly made by the hon. member for Lisgar and by bis friends from Manitoba to the House to-day. There has been no complaint that the revising officers are unfair or partial. Every one admits that the lists in Manitoba are prepared by non-partisan officers whose decisions are subject to an appeal to the judges of the county court. The judges hold courts of revision and independent officers deal with these lists, a privilege which we have not to-day under the Liberal legislation of the province of Nova Scotia, although we have sought it many times. It has always been denied us both by the Liberal government of the province of Nova Scotia and by this government in respect to the Dominion lists in that province. To say that these lists, revised by judges of the land are to be passed over in Manitoba, and that the lists of Nova Scotia has, to which we have no right of appeal to any independent officers, are to be taken and accepted as absolutely fair and impartial does seem to me to be a proposition that would not commend itself to the judgment of some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House for whose fairness subject to certain partisan bias which we must always expect, I have every possible respect.
I do not think this discussion has been wasted to-day. Probably before the end of the session we may hear, as my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Staples) has said, a little more about that thin red line. We have some pretty7 full information about the way in which that line was utilized, and I do not think that everything has been said on this subject to-day which might be said in regard to it. For the present it is enough to say that I trust my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, does not intend to suggest to the House that there is to he one principle applied to the province of Manitoba because it happens to have a Conservative government or because its lists do not happen to be made out to the liking of some hon. gentlemen on the other

side of the House and another principle applied to other provinces.
Let me say before I sit down what I forgot to say before and it is this: The hon. member for Lisgar spoke of the lists made up in 1901 in the (Province of Manitoba as if they were designedly unfair lists to the Liberals of that province. He knows very well, every lion, gentleman from Manitoba knows very well, that the reason why these lists were not favourable to the Liberals was the simple reason that they took no part in the revision upon the promise of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton), then Minister of the Interior, that these lists were not to be the lists Upon which the general election was to be run. That is the reason why the lists were not favourable to the Liberals ; they took no part in the revision. It is not denied that a promise was made by the hon. member for Brandon that these lists would be disregarded, and that new partisan lists would be made up for the purposes of the Dominion elections. Then, Conservatives naturally said the Liberals had made a mistake in expecting that their party friends would go so far as was prophesied. Undoubtedly the lists were not originally as favourable to the Liberals of Manitoba as they would have been if they had attended to the revision in the ordinary way. But that which was not accomplished by the Liberals by means of attending to the revision, which they would have done under ordinary circumstances, was accomplished, I know not whether at the suggestion of the hon. member, for Brandon-I hope not-by this thin red line which has been spoken of this afternoon. They did not do it by means of legislature because they dare not bring that legislation before this House, but their party organizers and their party heelers did it by means of this thin red line that has been spoken of. That is the only difference. The end was accomplished after all. The lists were dealt with. They were not dealt with by legislation brought down and openly and fairly discussed in this House, but the end was accomplished by having every one of these lists placed in the hands of the Liberal organizer for Manitoba who carved them according to his own sweet will receiving them for that purpose out of the hands of the returning officers who are the servants of this parliament. I am not speaking of matters of hearsay. I am speaking of matters that were deposed to on oath by these returning officers in more than one case in the province of Manitoba. So that the thing was accomplished very well after all. not by legislation which some members of the administration shrank from bringing down, shrank from taking the responsibility of, but the thing was accomplished by having every one of these deputy returning officers hand in his list to a gentleman named Leach, the Liberal organizer for Manitoba, and Mr. Leach arranged these by means of his thin red line so that a majority of Liberals was returned at the election held in November last. The hon. member for Lisgar and two or three other hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House have the audacity and hardihood in the face of these facts to stand up in this House and complain of these lists in Manitoba. I do not wonder that the hon. member for Lisgar, after he had spoken, and after he had heard a portion only of the speech of my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche) left this House and showed the extraordinary interest which he takes in this subject, introduced by himself this afternoon without notice, by not putting in an appearance during the remainder of the day. This is all we have to say for the moment on the subject. That hon. gentleman, an old parliamentary hand, did not even have the courtesy to let us know on this side of the House that he proposed to bring up this important subject although we hear very often suggestions of lack of courtesy if any hon. gentleman on this side of the House introduces a much less important subject without giving notice to the Prime Minister or to the proper minister of the Crown. However, he has seen fit to pursue his own course and I venture to say in conclusion that he will hear something more on this subject before the session closes.

This is the first time I have had the honour of hearing the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Greenway), and I must say he has chosen a very unfortunate subject for his maiden speech and also a very unfortunate province in which to deliver such an address. The province of Ontario had some little knowledge of Liberal fairness in the preparation of lists, and we from Ontario can speak feelingly on that question. But I understand that the hon. gentleman has lately come down from the mountain, not like the prophet of old with radiant smiles, but with a scowl on his visage, because forsooth he met defeat in that constituency. Smarting under a keen sense of his discomfiture, he opens out the vials of his wrath on the Conservative government in Manitoba because that government did not satis-isfy him in its preparation of the lists ; and to-day, in conjunction with the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Jackson), he coolly proposes that this House shall make a difference when it comes to deal with provinces which return a Conservative majority as compared with those which have Liberal administrations. This surely is a very strange doctrine. When the Conservative party was in power, it had a franchise that was fair to all throughout the Dominion, but these gentlemen opposite, in their wisdom, saw fit to abrogate that law and disfranchise citizens who had enjoyed the right to vote for many years, many of whom, I may say, reside in my own county. These hon. gentlemen cancelled this franchise

law, and they did so because there were Liberal governments in every province of the Dominion at that tune. But now it appears that the province of Manitoba, having elected to return a Liberal Conservative administration, is ripe for a change, and we are told that the province of Ontario is nearly ripe for a similar change. Why is this ? Simply because the province of Ontario, by a majority of 38,000 at the last election, showed the Liberal party that the people of that province had had enough of their fairness. We know something in Ontario about the preparation of lists. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Greenway) waxes eloquent about the great disability the people of Manitoba are labouring under in going to register. Let me tell him that in Ontario that was the least difficulty we had to contend with. Our difficulties only began when we got to the registration office. It was then quite a feat to get a vote on the list. Who was the revising officer ? In every case fie was a political appointee-an official appointed for political purposes-and who was bound to pay the debt of gratitude he owed those who put him in office, by keeping every possible Conservative off the list. That is what was done in Ontario for twenty-five years. Whenever we wanted to get a man on, we had to have lawyers to fight his case inch by inch ; and after he got on the list, were his troubles over ? Not by a long way. They were only beginning.. He had to run the gauntlet of those who were offering money for his vote ; and if he had sufficient backbone to resist and got as far as the polls, what happened ? He was very possibly sworn, if it did not happen that his vote had already been presented by some one supporting these gentlemen. And when he did succeed in putting fiis ballot into the box, it sometimes happened that it was not a real box. Sometimes his ballot was put to one side and another ballot, marked for the man he did not vote for, put in its place. After that there was a good deal in the counting. We know that in some polling subdivisions, not 100 miles from the constituency I represent, where eighty-two voters swore they had voted for a certain candidate, only forty-two ballots for that candidate were found in ithe box. The warning of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. R. L. Borden) to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) who seemed to be somewhat carried away, was very timely. That hon. minister will find that there will be a considerable amount of indignation excited if he endeavours to apply to Manitoba or Ontario a rule he does not apply to the rest of the Dominion. We have had trouble enough fighting for our rights in the province of Ontario ; and having obtained them by a popular majority of 38,000, we shall not submit to their being taken from us. We can speak feelingly on this subject, because we have been groaning under the load for years. Tear after year we Mr. COCKSHUTT.
have met defeat at the polls in that province -and why ? Not because the people were against us, but because we were smitten by an unseen hand, because we were robbed of our franchise, because we were deprived of our rights as citizens. That is no invention of my own. It has been told in the public glare of the courts to the disgrace of the Liberal party. These things have been revealed in our courts and condemned by our judges from one end of the province to the other. And after our ballots had been cast, and were likely to be called for in court, we know that in some cases they were burned by mistake. These gentlemen, who have raised this question to-day, have struck a very sore spot. Those gentlemen who have given us such broad hints that they are going to make a law which will apply to certain provinces because they are Conservative and will not apply to others because they are Liberal, will find they have struck a snag which this country will not stand. We are all willing to play the game and play it fairly. If we stay in opposition as long as our lives last, we are ready to do it so long as our elections are clean and free from reproach; but when the majority of the people say they want a certain man or party in power, we think it is time that man and party were put in power. These gentlemen talk of the grievance in Manitoba but they have not shown that the Conservative party has any advantage over the Liberals. If a Conservative has to travel 260 miles to get his franchise, why should not a Liberal do the same ? There is no difference in that respect between the two, but this thin red line makes a difference. It strikes the Conservatives only and the Liberals escape. IIow is it that the thin red line is applied to one party and not to the other ? If you have to apply it at all, apply it in fairness, and we will make no complaint. We are a comparatively small band on this side-not as big as we should be according to the wishes of the country, not representatives of the number of people who voted Conservative by any means- but that comparatively small band is not going to have its rights lightly trodden upon. The hon. gentleman has evinced a great desire to propitiate minorities, but only minorities of a certain kind. When the Conservative party was in a minority, did they show any such desire ? Not a bit of it. Every unfair advantage that could be taken was taken for 25 years in the province of Ontario by these gentlemen ; but I am thankful to say that at last we have there an upright, straight government. What was the very first act of that government ? It was to strike out that marked ballot, which hon. gentlemen held up for twenty-five years as a whip over their party friends and nonparty friends to keep them in line. Mr. Whitney, however, has done away with it. He has said : Gentlemen, whether you are for us or against us, we do not wish to

know ; your vote is your own ; poll it like a man ; and if you do we shall count it for the man for whom it was cast. These gentlemen who come down to this House to preach about Liberal fairness in elections little know what the province of Ontario has had to endure for the last twenty-five years and how it has had to fight for its rights.
The very first act of the Conservative government has been to say : Gentlemen, we will not take any unfair advantage through that marked ballot ; that marked ballot goes ; no matter which party you belong to you can vote by secret ballot, and you can put it into a proper ballot box, and it will be counted for the candidate you intended it for. I am sorry to say that system did not exist in Ontario under the Liberal regime. My hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Porter) can tell a tale of what happened in some constituencies last election ; he can tell what was meant by the Liberal boast, that no power on earth could defeat the Liberal party. I leave you, Mr. Speaker, to judge where the power would come from that could defeat the Liberal party. That hon. gentleman from Hastings can show the ballot box that was falsely made for the purpose of destroying the freeman's franchise. Surely the member for Lisgar is out of touch with the province in which he at present is, and if he Las returned sorely disappointed from Mountain, why should he pour out his vials of wrath in this House against the people of Manitoba because their Franchise Law does not happen to please him ? He had his way for a time. His government did wrong, and they are out of power, and they are suffering for doing wrong. Under our constitution governments come and governments go if there is fair-play, and X presume that if this government is disappointed in North Oxford and London, you will hear some of these gentlemen opposite doing as the member for Selkirk does, and asking for a special law making an exception of Ontario, so far as the Franchise Act is concerned. Mr. Speaker, the snow will certainly fly before the House prorogues if any such outrage as that is attempted.

I am sure the government will be gjad to know now what their duty is, and that before they attempt to pass auy law they will have to go to the hon. member for Carieton (Mr. It. L. Borden) and to the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) and ask them to please be allowed to pass it. A government with seventy-five or eighty majority in this House must go to these gentlemen and ask them, forsooth, if it pleases their mighty-ness and their holiness to be allowed to pass a law. I would like to know who is running this country. Is it this little outfit over there, this small little band that the people of Canada rejected ; these men who were
told by the people from the Atlantic to the Pacific, told that their policy was wrong and that they were not fit to govern ? Is it these men who are going to hold the House up until the snow flies ?
Some hon. MEMBElRiS. Yes.

Two can play at that game. We can stay here as long as they can, and we will do it, too. What this government undertakes to do they are going to do, and they are not going to ask the opposition whether they can do it or not. It is a nice thing if the minority, a small minority, that is discredited by the people, that the people have spewed out of their mouths ; it is a nice thing if they can hold this parliament in session until the snow flies. The leader of the opposition has given us warning ; he has threatened us in plain terms : You cannot pass this law unless it pleases* us, Who is ' us ' I would like to know ? A little discredited band over there who, if they went back to the country to-day, small as they are, they would come back with scarcely a baker's dozen ; a miserable outfit. And the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt), he has not been long in this House, and when he is in the House a few years longer, he will not be so bold and so bumptious as lie has been to-night. He talks about the province of Ontario. What have we suffered from in the province of Ontario ?
Ross.

Ross ! Ross and his party ruled this country for thirty-three year's, and I venture to say you will not rule it for thirty-three years or half that period. You were going to reform everything ; you said that the departments were reeking with corruption ; you have failed to show it, and the only thing Mr. Whitney has done is to repeal the marked ballot. That is a ballot that has been in force in England for generations, and which the people of England believe is a good ballot, and I do not care whether the Whitney government repeals it or not. He was going to repeal the Conmee Act and the Succession Duties Act, but instead of that he increased the succession duties. He has not been able to show one single thing that the Ross government has done that has not been to the credit of the province of Ontario. There never was a province governed so wisely or so well as the province of Ontario under the Liberal government, whose record will go down to generations as a wise and an honest government. There have been no complaints about the election law in the province of Ontario. The list is taken from the assessment roll and an appeal lies to the county judge, a court of revision is held, and Liberals and Conservatives have fair-play before that court. Everything is fairly and honestly conducted, and there are no complaints. There were complaints of the

Dominion Franchise Act in the old days, when the lion, member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) and his friends got 200 Indians put on the voters' lists to vote 'for him. We all remember how Dr. Montague appealed to the Indians in Haldimand to vote for him because the Queen wanted them to do so. That is the way these gentlemen opposite conducted elections. And the member for Brantford has the audacity and the cheek to rise in this House and to denounce the system now in force in the province of Ontario. I venture to say you cannot improve on the way the voters' lists are made up in that province. It was not so under the old Franchise Act. I remember in the county of Kent when there were 1,100 appeals sent in, and the judge-he was a revising barrister then and not a judge-refused to hear these appeals at all, and -we had to go to the 'fcourts in Toronto to get a mandamus to compel him to hear them. That is the way things were then conducted in the county of Kent, as I know to my sorrow, and in various other places in the province of Ontario the lists were made up in the most outrageous and partisan manner. To-day the hon. member for Selkirk has shown that men have to go 200 miles to get their names on the list. Is that not a monstrous thing ? I do not care whether it is against the Conservatives or the Liberals ; 1 think it most unfair, and never ought to be allowed to exist.
What sense of fairness or justice is there in that ? Sixty or seventy miles and then only allowing 13 hours of one day for each municipality. Why Sir, it is utterly impossible that they should get all the names on in that time. I remember in the town of Toronto Junction last year there were no less than 1,200 appeals for names to be added and struck off and the list is made up every year. I suppose there is one-half *that number in Manitoba in any constituency, it would be utterly impossible in 13 hours to answer all the questions asked there and get the names put on or off, and so I say if such a state of affairs exists there, as has been described here to-day it is the bounden duty of the government to look into the matter and rectify any wrong that may exist. When the Tories get into power in any province they always follow their own way and conduct things in a partisan manner. They did it in the 18 years they were in power in the Dominion when we had that iniquitous franchise law, that was expensive, that put the people to a great deal of trouble and expense and which when this government came into power they properly repealed and placed the franchise as it is to-day. If they are going to repeat these tactics in Manitoba and m Ontario-in Ontario they have not done anything yet-but we will see what they will do in a year or two and I say if they are going to follow out these tactics then it is time for this government to interfere and repair that wrong. No case could be stronger than that made out by

the hon. member for Lisgar and those who have spoken from this side of the House, and have stated that men have to go 60, 70 and even 200 miles to register their votes. I say it is an outrage upon the people that should not be allowed to exist any longer than it takes to repeal it, and if the case is as made out by these gentlemen then I say it is the bounden duty of the government to interfere and rectify that wrong.
From the sadness in the tone of the hon. member for Centre York it is quite plain he has met with a fatal blow.
No, he has not.

Every one in this House, particularly members from Toronto, know the fatal blow he got in the last few days and what made it doubly bad is that it has come from Mr. Whitney. The hon. gentleman has in his constituency a place called Toronto Junction, which under the guidance care of the Ross administration has been the resort of ail the toughs and thieves who used it for the purpose of gambling.
It is not in my constituency at all.
Toronto Junction ?
No.

I am going to give the hon. member for Centre York credit for one thing and that is gratitude. The kindly acts that were performed for him in past elections by this gang when in Centre York and when Toronto Junction was in Centre York are not forgotten by him and that is the reason he is wailing to-night that that gang of iniquity is toroken up.
It never was in Centre York.

It was in the riding the hon. gentleman represented and lie got the benefit of their influence, and that influence was fostered by the Ross government by reason of the fact that it got very great benefits from keeping that gang there. It is rather hard that what has happened in Ontario has happened, that for the first time in 30 years the criminal law has been administered. That is what galls these hon. gentlemen and the member for Centre York knows it better than any one. Is it not galling to think that on the 13th in London there will be no more plug-gers ? Mr. Quinn is now serving a year in the Central Prison ; he voted five times for Hyman in the last election. Mr. Whitney has not done anything ? The criminal law in Ontario was paralysed and Quinn walked around the streets of London boasting of what he had done. That has all been changed and Quinn is now in prison. Where are the forms that used to go about tiie corridors here. Geo. B. Grey and Shipley and Lott, where are they? Under this awful man Whitney they are on the other

side now, in the United States, and the member for Centre York no longer grasps the hand and sees the burly form of Lott as he walks dropping a pointer as to the ballot boxes that were going to toe used and stating that it is out of the power of Providence to defeat them when these boxes were used. Mr. Whitney has broken up the junction pool room and he started the criminal law in motion. Messrs. Lott and Shipley regret it and he is making it so hot that even ' Cap. ' Sullivan will not be at the station to wish the member for Centre York good luck in his trip to Ottawa and the ' Minnie M ' has gone out of service as well. The member for Centre York must not say that Mr. Whitney has done nothing ; he has certainly done something, he has started the criminal law in motion and we give you fair notice that in the election in London the criminal law will be enforced and the gang you have had floating from one province to another who were in Brockville, in a wonderful election, and in West Elgin and all over Ontario are not to be found now. The ringleaders Lott and Shipley have disappeared. Let the government make their appeals in London on the 13th and they will have to go with the Ross government. There is no danger of this gang being in London. My hon. friends opposite are to lose the benefit of that beautiful entourage which followed them throughout the province. I think mv hon. friend had better say less about Whitney. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that there are some very uneasy friends of hon. gentlemen opposite who have had large dealings with the Crown Lands Department. It takes time always to stir up these things but you will hear of them later, they are coming and they are not coming the way of some Grit lumbermen who for years have been living on the fat of the land through, the Crown Lands Department of Ontario. We have heard the old story about the infamous Dominion voters' list in Ontario. What was the fact in reference to that ? My hon. friend says there were 1,100 appeals. All who know him know that everything he says has to be discounted. He was wrong in saying that there were 2,000 Indian electors in South Brant. Every one knew that this is untrue and I suppose we will have to take the same discount off his statement as to the number of appeals in a certain election. As there are about 200 Indian electors, so I presume there were about 110 appeals and there are equally as many appeals under the local law as there were formerly, the same judges hold the courts. The main and the greatest difficultv about that is that under the old Act the Indians had votes but under the present Act they have not. How many constituencies does that affect in Ontario or the whole Dominion ? The Minister of Customs could be elected in the riding of Brant when there were Indian voters but he got licked in that riding
and he is afraid to go back to it when there are no Indian voters there, so the Minister of Customs must have got the benefit of the Indian vote. We are not going to be threatened, we can stay here as long as hon. gentlemen can. Goodness knows the hon. gentleman is a patient waiter. The hon. gentleman has been waiting since 1896 to be taken into this cabinet. The newspapers from time to time announce that he is going in as the minister of this or the minister of that. But he is never going in as the minister of anything, as a matter of fact, and for the simple reason that he could not be re-elected for Centre York if he were taken into the cabinet.
IIow do you know ?

The hon. gentleman is afraid to try it. But, after London is disposed of, he may have a chance, that is, unless the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman) is to have another chance in Prescott or in Russell where there may be some reasonable prospect of his being re-elected.
He will be re-elected in London.

The hon. member for Brockville (Mr Derbyshire) said the other night that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hyman) would be elected. And he undertook to prove it in a way peculiarly his own-he was prepared to bet any amount of money on it. Now, I hope my hon. friend (Mr. Derbyshire) will go up to London in this campaign ; because as soon as his burly form is pointed out and people are told that he is the man who wishes to bet money on the success of the government party in this election, they will come about him like flies around honey. And, if he will follow Mr. Hyman in the house-to-house canvass that he is making, the people may think that they can have a nickel dropped in the slot. But I warn him that the Londoners will not be satisfied with nickels in this election. They know that the government is playing for its last stake and that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Hyman) must be elected at all hazards, and so one-dollar or two-dollar bills will be utterly useless. In proportion to the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Derbyshire's) dimensions, the bill should be correspondingly large. I do not know whether this government intends to bring in a special Bill for the benefit of the demoralized Grit party in Manitoba or not. If they do, we shall examine that Bill and see wliat it contains. Of course, according to the old saying, desperate diseases require desperate remedies, and the condition of the Liberal party in Manitoba is such that one hardly knows whether to speak of it as a party at all or not. They had a by-election in Mountain the other day, and every one knows the result. I think there are three or four opponents of the Roblin government in the legislature, and they have been tumbling over one another, since the last election,

to get in with the government side. What is the complaint that has been voiced here this afternoon ? It is that they are not going to have a thorough revision of the lists in Manitoba this year. Why, there will be no revision of the lists in Ontario this year. Hon. gentlemen on either side do not care to spend their time and money fixing up the lists in Ontario. And I will tell you why : It is because we know there will be no election. There will be no Dominion election- that is a certainty. Every man who sits in this House can console himself with the reflection that this government is not going to meet the people until the last moment. And, as to the Ontario legislature, there is not a possibility of there being an election there for four years. You could not even galvanize the parties^ into preparing to have an election this year. For you cannot have an election unless there is an opposition, and there is no opposition in the Ontario legislature to-day. The opposition did not challenge a vote in the House last session.

They did-on the Gamey matter. They challenged a vote on the white-wash and it was a big coat of white-wash too.
eminent doing to-day ? It is delaying the session to prevent business being done. They will not let business go on. They have here this coercion Bill, but they do not move an inch forward, but they put up these tricks to delay. One after another their supporters fire their guns and retire. Was it not a pathetic sight to see the burly form of the hon. member for Lisgar, after he had emptied the vials of bis wrath upon this side, retiring from the chamber while the sympathetic onlookers could almost hear the refrain of that beautiful and touching song ' Don't you go Tommy, Don't go.' They are delaying the business of the House. Let them give us this coercion Bill that we may get on with it, finish our business and go home. Let the people of London and North Oxford know what the government's policy is. Let them know whether this is a Bill, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) says it is, with little or nothing in it, or a Bill as the hon. member from Centre York (Mr. Campbell) says it is, so harmless that the system of separate schools will die out in a little time, or a Bill as some other hon. gentlemen on that side say it is, that will place on the statute-book and establish for all time the strongest system of separate schools ever known in the Dominion.
, Mr. BENNETT. True ; I had forgotten about the Gamey business. But I should thought that after the knock out that Mr. Gamey gave the Liberal government in Ontario we would never have heard his name from a Liberal again.
In conclusion, let me commiserate my hon. friend from Centre York on his dwindling and vanishing majority. His speech reminded me of that grand old hymn :
Hark ! From the tombs a doleful sound That bids my soul arise.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) ought to be ashamed to mention his name.

I do not wonder that my hon. friend from East Peterborough (Mr. Finlay) is roused to some kind of protest when the name of Mr. Gahiey is mentioned. Why, the hon. gentleman's political godfather was Jimmy Stratton. And I am here to-night to acknowledge that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Finlay) has one good quality the quality^ of gratitude. He cannot but feel a sympathetic pang when he hears mentioned the name of the man who struck Jimmy Stratton in the vital parts, the man who placed Mr. James Stratton where he it, to-day-outside the pale of Ontario politics, outside the pale even of the Liberal party, for in that party to-day there are none so poor to do him reverence.
If the government bring in this Bill, we will be here to see what it contains. But so long as the people of Manitoba are almost unanimous in favour of the present government, this House should hesitate to say that a law passed at the instance of a government so firmly entrenched in the approval of the people of Manitoba is a bad law. We will wait and see what the government do. And we must be prepared to wait, for this government seems to be a | waiting government. For, what is the gov-Mr. BENNETT.
I know the hon. gentleman's deep feeling of sympathy for his old friends in Toronto Junction, who, by the prompt and stern action of Premier Whitney have been wiped out, their pool-room closed up and the hon. gentleman's band of tried and trusty followers scattered to the four winds of Heaven.

Why is this chargeable to income instead of capital ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Public buildings of this character are not charged to capital. Public buildings at Ottawa relating to the government are charged to capital, but other public buildings throughout the country are not.

Is this the only public building for the whole province of New Brunswick ?
!Mr. FIELDING. This is not an estimate for the future, it is closing up the current year's accounts. Estimates are coming in that have to be dealt with separately.
By the application of what principle does the hon. gentleman charge a building to income, and a dredge to capital ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I suppose my hon. friend is referring to dredging the St. Lawrence. It has been the custom to charge certain dredging, especially a channel like the St. Lawrence to capital. It might be difficult to give a logical reason for charging that to capital and not to income ; but the Englishman's reason for these things is : That is always the way we have been accustomed to do it.
i
Is the present government satisfied to accept precedents in all such matters without making any change ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No : but there is something to be said in favour of this practice. Dredging the St. Lawrence is part of a great national undertaking, which should be distinct from an ordinary small building. At all events, that is the rule which we have adopted in the past. I have not had my attention drawn to the necessity for a change, but I do not think, at first blush, it follows that a change should be made.	.
I am willing to admit that the result of the work of a dredge is properly chargeable to capital account ; I question whether the instrument or tool that performs the work can.be rightly so charged.
